old: Integrated information decomposition (ΦID) with the minimum-mutual-information (MMI) redundancy function underlies most fMRI synergy reports. We derive in closed form the sixteen Gaussian-MMI atoms of two first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) processes coupled only at lag 0. With equal coefficients the synergy atom sts equals both self-prediction atoms plus the double redundancy, balanced by four negative atoms; with unequal coefficients MMI takes the smaller self-information and sts falls below that sum. sts therefore inherits self-information's dependence on lag-1 autocorrelation r₁: at these data's operating point, 0.01 of r₁ moves it by 0.061 nats and 0.1 of the lag-0 correlation |q| by 0.019 (4.7 to 1 per standard deviation across pairs; 1.4 to 1 for the windowed estimator), while lagged coupling moves it non-monotonically. In within-subject fMRI of 14 volunteers given N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) and placebo, the primary contrast, the pre/post difference-in-differences of whole-brain MMI-sts, was planned to test an increase; its statistic was fixed after global fits on the same data had shown a decrease. MMI-sts fell (−0.081 nats [−0.132, −0.031], p = 0.004, 13 of 14) with r₁, close to the −0.094 of a generator with the data's spectrum and the same fall of r₁; across subjects the two changes share most of their reliable variance (disattenuated r 0.95 [0.62, 0.99]). The regional sts map follows regional r₁ (r = 0.86). Recomputed with AR(1) cross-lags at each pair's measured autocorrelations and lag-0 correlation, sts falls by 0.0115 more than observed, against 0.003–0.005 in simulated pure autocorrelation changes (p = 0.11–0.25); the difference cannot be attributed on these data. Under the common-change-in-surprisal (CCS) redundancy function the synergy atom is near zero and nearly flat in r₁ on the family, and prewhitening cannot fully remove the dependence from band-passed data. We recommend reporting r₁ beside sts and each sts contrast beside its AR(1)-substituted estimate.
new: Integrated information decomposition (ΦID) with the minimum-mutual-information (MMI) redundancy function underlies most fMRI synergy reports we found. We derive in closed form the sixteen Gaussian-MMI atoms of two first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) processes coupled only at lag 0. With equal coefficients the synergy atom sts is both self-prediction atoms plus the double redundancy; with unequal coefficients it is less. sts inherits self-information's dependence on lag-1 autocorrelation r₁: at the data's operating point 0.01 of r₁ moves it by 0.061 nats, 0.1 of the lag-0 correlation |q| by 0.019 (4.7 to 1 per within-window standard deviation; neither is lagged coupling, which can move it either way). In within-subject fMRI of 14 volunteers given N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) and placebo — a proof of concept, its statistic fixed after whole-run fits of these data showed a decrease — whole-brain MMI-sts fell relative to placebo (difference-in-differences −0.081 [−0.132, −0.031], p = 0.004, 13 of 14; −0.054 adjusted for the runs' pre-injection gap) with r₁, near a generator's −0.094 for that fall; across subjects the two DMT-minus-placebo differences covary (cross-half r 0.69 [0.26, 0.89], disattenuated 0.95), partly through that gap. Regional sts follows regional r₁ (r = 0.86). With AR(1) cross-lags substituted at each pair's measured autocorrelations and lag-0 correlation, sts falls 0.0115 more than observed, 0.006–0.009 above simulated pure autocorrelation changes: a test detecting 0.0155 does not resolve this (p = 0.11–0.25), but across subjects it scales with the r₁ change more steeply than either generator under the subjects' own changes (no replicate as steep); its source is unidentified. Under the common-change-in-surprisal (CCS) redundancy function the atom is near zero and, on the family, nearly flat in r₁; prewhitening removes r₁ only at orders leaving mostly stop-band residue, where a smaller contrast remains. We recommend reporting r₁ beside sts and each contrast beside its AR(1)-substituted estimate.
why: Abstract: A's w3 (the proof-of-concept register), w4 and C's w4 (the ratio's inputs, within a window), m3 ('can move'); B's MAJOR 1 (the adjusted contrast beside the DiD), MAJOR 2 (the cross-half correlation with its interval as the headline, the two DMT-minus-placebo differences, the pre-injection gap), MAJOR 3 and A's M1 (the per-subject comparison with the matched generators, B28, with its shares), MINOR 1 and W5 (the excess and the minimal detectable difference, B27: the excesses as a range at three decimals, the detectable difference at the table's four), MINOR 4 and A's m4 (prewhitening, B16c: r₁ is removed only at the orders that leave mostly stop-band residue, and a smaller contrast remains there); C's m7 ('most fMRI synergy reports we found': eight of the ten studies state MMI) and m19 (at most 300 words). The cross-half correlation's interval is printed from its six-decimal value (`derived_r24.out`, item 6: [0.258078, 0.894889]), the CCS clause names the family, on which the flatness is shown (Results 6), and 'whole-run fits' is said for the global fits.

old: Functional brain imaging asks how regions carry information together, not only which are active. A widely used measure, from integrated information decomposition, is synergy: information that a pair of regions holds jointly and neither holds alone. Synergy has been reported to differ across the cortex, and integrated information, in regions ranked by their synergy, to fall under anaesthesia and in disorders of consciousness. We show, on a solvable family and in one brain-imaging dataset, that with the estimator most of these studies use the synergy value is mostly something simpler: how well each region's signal predicts its own next sample, its autocorrelation. The dataset is from fourteen volunteers scanned under the psychedelic DMT and placebo. Under DMT the autocorrelation of the signals fell, and the measured synergy fell by about as much as a simulation with the data's properties gives for that fall; across volunteers the two falls went together. We had set out to test the opposite hypothesis, that DMT raises synergy as this estimator measures it; the measure fell instead, and we report why. We recommend that studies report autocorrelation beside synergy and compare each synergy contrast with the estimate our closed form gives from the regions' autocorrelations.
new: A widely used measure of how brain regions carry information together, from integrated information decomposition, is synergy: information that a pair of regions holds jointly and neither holds alone. Synergy has been reported to differ across the cortex, and integrated information in synergy-ranked regions to fall under anaesthesia and in disorders of consciousness. We show, on a solvable family and in one dataset, that with the estimator these studies use the synergy value's level, its pattern across regions and its change between conditions follow something simpler: how well each region's signal predicts its own next sample, its autocorrelation. The dataset is fourteen volunteers scanned under the psychedelic DMT and placebo. Under DMT, relative to placebo, the signals' autocorrelation fell and the measured synergy fell by about as much as a simulation with the data's properties gives for that fall; across volunteers the two differences went together (synergy rose in one volunteer, autocorrelation in two). We had set out to test the opposite hypothesis, that DMT raises synergy; it fell instead, and we report why. We recommend that studies report autocorrelation beside synergy and compare each synergy contrast with the estimate our closed form gives from each pair's autocorrelations and correlation.
why: Author summary: C's m5 ('relative to placebo') and m16 (the bound on 'mostly': the level, the regional pattern and the contrast); B's MAJOR 2 and the rule of B27's entry (iii) (two DMT-minus-placebo differences, the subjects in which either rose: subject 14's sts and subjects 5's and 14's r₁ DiDs are positive). The last sentence names the estimate's inputs as the Abstract does, each pair's autocorrelations and its correlation (the committed sentence named the autocorrelations alone). For the 200-word limit the committed first sentence ('Functional brain imaging asks how regions carry information together, not only which are active') is merged into the second, which keeps its subject and drops 'not only which are active'; 200 words.

old: Barrett (2015) exhibited positive net synergy — hence positive MMI synergy, since MMI redundancy is non-negative — in a dynamical Gaussian example in which a target's own immediate past is one of the sources (his Example 1); the net synergy vanishes when the infinite pasts are the sources, while the MMI synergy stays at ½ ln(1 + α²) (his Eqs. 73 and 79–82). MMI's aggregate synergy, the same four-atom sum, cannot tell a synergistic pair from two independent autocorrelated processes (Varley, 2024, Eqs. 4–6 and 12), and PID applied to time series rests on an assumption of independent, identically distributed samples that is often violated (Faes et al., 2025). Exact Gaussian decompositions exist for transfer entropy (Faes et al., 2017), for static systems (Barrett, 2015; Kay & Ince, 2018) and for single-target lagged PIDs of multivariate autoregressive processes with a target's own past among the sources (Barrett, 2015, Sec. V), Varley (2024) gave the aggregate identity for a disintegrated pair, and the ΦID authors' worked example is a coupled autoregressive pair (Mediano et al., 2021, Fig. 5 and Appendix VI); what none of them gives is the sixteen atoms in closed form, and so which of them take their value from the self-information, how sts depends on a pair's lag-1 autocorrelation r₁ and lag-0 correlation q, where real region pairs sit on that dependence, whether CCS shares the property, and how much of an observed sts change the pairs' own autocorrelations carry.

old: This study did not set out to provide these. It was planned as a directional test of whether whole-brain synergy, measured as MMI-sts, is up-regulated under N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT), a drug that produces a state of intensified conscious content; the predicted increase was motivated by the synergistic-workspace account, in which loss of consciousness goes with reduced ΦR within the workspace (Luppi et al., 2024). The record states the hypothesis before its first check on the data, an order the version history cannot confirm; the test statistic was fixed after whole-run ('global') fits on the same data had already shown a decrease (Methods). MMI-sts decreased; the decrease was carried by the pairs' self-prediction atoms and went with the lag-1 autocorrelation contrast, and the closed form was derived afterwards, motivated by the same data, to account for it. The Results give the closed form for two first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) processes coupled only at lag 0 (1), the DMT contrast (2), the regional map (3), an estimate from each pair's own autocorrelations and lag-0 correlation (4), the lag dependence (5), CCS (6) and remedies (7). Apart from the primary contrast every analysis is exploratory, and the account itself is post hoc.

old: Notation: an atom's letters give the kind of past and future information (r redundant, x or y unique to region X or Y, s synergistic); values are in nats; a difference-in-differences (DiD) is (post − pre) on DMT minus (post − pre) on placebo, per subject. Lag-1 autocorrelation r₁ is estimated two ways: regional r₁, a region's sample lag-1 autocorrelation within a window (its mean over regions is whole-brain r₁), and pair r₁, the mean of a pair's two lag-1 correlations in its window's 4 × 4 correlation matrix, the quantity the simulations report and the AR(1)-substituted estimate uses; on the family both equal a. W = 60 denotes the primary estimator's 60-TR windows.
new: Notation: an atom's letters give the kind of past and future information (r redundant, x or y unique to region X or Y, s synergistic); values are in nats; a difference-in-differences (DiD) is (post − pre) on DMT minus (post − pre) on placebo, per subject. Lag-1 autocorrelation r₁ is estimated two ways: regional r₁, a region's sample lag-1 autocorrelation within a window (its mean over regions is whole-brain r₁), and pair r₁, the mean of a pair's two lag-1 correlations, a_x and a_y, in its window's 4 × 4 correlation matrix, the quantity the simulations report and the AR(1)-substituted estimate uses; on the family both equal a. The AR(1)-substituted estimate of an atom is its value in the pair's 4 × 4 correlation matrix with the two lag-0 entries set to their mean q and the two measured cross-lag correlations replaced by their AR(1) values, a_y q and a_x q (Methods). W = 60 denotes the primary estimator's 60-TR windows, and a global fit one fit over a whole run.

old: Whole-brain MMI-sts fell under DMT, and across subjects its fall went with the fall of lag-1 autocorrelation. The primary contrast of this paper is the pre-specified DiD of whole-brain MMI-sts on the primary variant and estimator (Table 2): −0.0809 nats [−0.1317, −0.0310], exact sign-flip p = 0.0038, negative in 13 of 14 subjects, −7.0 % of the pre-injection DMT mean; −0.0649 [−0.1010, −0.0260] after residualisation on framewise displacement. It was planned as a test of an increase of whole-brain MMI-sts at W = 60, and under the directional-failure rule the significant decrease refutes that hypothesis as operationalised; on the account of Results 1 it bears on MMI-sts, not on synergy in the intended sense. The rule and the test statistic were written after global fits on the same data had shown a decrease (Methods), so the windowed contrast measures, with a second estimator, an effect already seen. The contrast held without global signal regression (−0.1031 [−0.1629, −0.0435], p = 0.0026), at W = 30 (−0.0686, p = 0.0042), on windows 5–14 (−0.0733, p = 0.0070; S1 Table) and in each of the 14 leave-one-out refits on each variant (p ≤ 0.008); the global fit, the estimate seen before the test was written, gives −0.0801 [−0.1362, −0.0251], p = 0.0071.
new: Whole-brain MMI-sts fell under DMT relative to placebo, and across subjects the two DMT-minus-placebo differences, of sts and of lag-1 autocorrelation, went together. The primary contrast is the pre-specified DiD of whole-brain MMI-sts on the primary variant and estimator (Table 2): −0.0809 nats [−0.1317, −0.0310], exact sign-flip p = 0.0038, negative in 13 of 14 subjects, −7.0 % of the pre-injection DMT mean. It was planned as a test of an increase: the increase failed whatever the two-sided p, and under the directional-failure rule the significant decrease refutes the hypothesis as operationalised. Its two-sided statistic was fixed after global fits on the same data had shown the decrease (Methods), and on the account of Results 1 it bears on MMI-sts, not on synergy in the intended sense. The DiD is one of three readings (Table 2): the runs' pre-injection gap, DMT minus placebo, +0.0176 (p = 0.2307), lies in the direction that enlarges the DiD (the scrutiny S2 Text applies to the deconvolved ΦR contrast); the post-injection gap is −0.0633 (p = 0.0001, negative in 14 of 14); and the baseline-adjusted contrast, the post-injection gap expected at a pre-injection gap of zero, is −0.0544 [−0.0806, −0.0283]. The DiD's between-subject variance is mostly the gap's (the DiD's SD 0.0887 against the post-injection gap's 0.0485; r(DiD, pre-injection gap) = −0.888, r² = 0.79), and the one positive DiD belongs to the subject with the most negative gap. The DiD stays the primary statistic, as pre-specified; it estimates the drug's effect only if the runs' pre-injection difference would have persisted. The contrast held on the sensitivity variant (Table 2), at W = 30 (−0.0686, p = 0.0042), on windows 5–14 (−0.0733, p = 0.0070; S1 Table) and, post hoc, in each leave-one-out refit on each variant (p ≤ 0.008); the global fit, seen before the test was written, gives −0.0801 [−0.1362, −0.0251], p = 0.0071.

A pure autocorrelation change also produces a positive residual, because the sampling scatter of the cross-lag correlations lowers the observed sts below the estimate by an amount that grows with pair r₁ and |q|. In simulations with a fall of 0.012–0.015 in pair r₁ applied to the DMT run only (Methods; S3 Text §6, its residual table; S10 Table), the residual DiD is +0.0027 ± 0.0014 on a band-passed generator with the data's spectrum and +0.0049 ± 0.0017 on AR(1) pairs; on a finite-sample null solved to the data's pair r₁ in each run and period it is +0.0054 (Methods). The data's residual DiD is not distinguished from these three (exact p = 0.108, 0.218 and 0.251), but the test is weak: with the residual DiD's SE of 0.0051 nats over subjects a t test detects, at 80 % power, a difference of 0.0155 nats from a point expectation, against excesses of 0.0088, 0.0066 and 0.0061, and each expectation is treated as a known constant. The per-subject comparison carries more (Table 3, whose caption gives the regressors; Fig 3c): the generators' rates per unit of pair r₁, −0.18, −0.39 and −0.37 (S3 Text §6), are ratios of means under one change of r₁, and the closer comparison is each generator's slope across simulated subjects whose autocorrelation changes are the data's. The data's slope, −0.75 per unit of r₁ DiD (t interval [−1.13, −0.37]), lies below the central 95 % of every condition's slopes: a pure autocorrelation change of the data's heterogeneity does not produce the data's per-subject scaling on either generator; it stays negative with any one or two subjects left out and without subject 8, subject 14 or both, the extreme r₁ changes (Table 3), and the ramp moves the generators' mean residual DiD by 0.0001 and 0.0006 nats from the step (unrounded means). At the group level the ratio of means, −0.79 per unit of whole-brain r₁ (−0.74 per unit of pair r₁, from the printed means), has a Fieller interval of [−1.60, −0.08] (g = 0.61), which contains all three rates; the per-subject relation's cross-half correlations are −0.700 and −0.385 on the primary variant and −0.598 and −0.051 on the sensitivity variant (S3 Text §6).

old: Prewhitening cannot fully remove the dependence from band-passed data. BOLD band-passed to 0.01–0.08 Hz holds 99.2 % of its power in the band, and at TR 2 s any series confined to the band has r₁ ≥ cos(2π × 0.08 Hz × 2 s) = 0.54 (flat in-band noise has 0.82), so a whitened series with r₁ below 0.54 must carry power outside the band, which the whitening filter can only have amplified from the stop-band residue. AR(p) residuals (p by the Bayesian information criterion, BIC, in 1–5, at the cap for 3,218 of 3,220 series) keep r₁ = 0.26 and 34 % of their power above the band, against 0.1 % in the raw series; MMI-sts on them is 0.22, its contrast −0.026 [−0.064, +0.011] (p = 0.14); AR(1) residuals keep r₁ = 0.75 and a contrast of −0.062 (p = 0.0006). Prewhitening also has costs: on Human Connectome Project (HCP) fMRI a mutual-information test's false-positive rate rose from 42 % to over 88 % after AR(p) prewhitening (Cliff et al., 2021); making a BOLD series entirely uncorrelated may remove neuronal information carried by the haemodynamic response, a concern Honari et al. (2019) raise although their own simulation found no detrimental effect; and band-pass filtering itself reintroduces autocorrelation (Arbabshirani et al., 2014).

### The fall of r₁ under DMT

Why r₁ fell is not identified here, and the fall is not an artefact: the atom's dependence on r₁ is the estimator's property; the fall of r₁ is a property of the data and may be the drug's effect on the signal. On the same dataset the data authors refer to DMT's "decreased autocorrelation between adjacent BOLD activity" and "increased temporal entropy" (Singleton et al., 2025, SI Figure 14); under DMT the EEG's signal diversity rises and its alpha power falls (Timmermann et al., 2019, 2023), as MEG signal diversity rises under psilocybin, ketamine and LSD, most in its temporal form (Schartner et al., 2017); here the regional autocorrelation function decays faster under DMT (Results 5), and within the DMT run the whole-brain TDMI, a function of r₁ alone on the family, fell as the EEG's Lempel–Ziv complexity rose (per-subject Spearman ρ over 28 bins −0.24, percentile interval [−0.40, −0.08], one-sided p = 0.002 against a phase-randomised null; on the placebo run −0.05, p = 0.22, or −0.09, p = 0.045, without global signal regression), a prediction recorded before it was computed (S1 Text; S6 Table), though a coherence the shared drug time course alone could produce. A faster-decaying BOLD autocorrelation is the fMRI form of that family of findings; we found no published application of ΦID to psychedelic data (Methods; S3 Text §10; Liardi et al., 2025, is a PID on MEG under LSD, ketamine and psilocybin). Non-neural routes are open too: DMT raises blood pressure and heart rate on the time course of its subjective effects (Strassman & Qualls, 1994); framewise displacement was higher under DMT than under placebo after the injection (Timmermann et al., 2023, Methods and SI Appendix, Fig. S4; its DiD here +0.0143, p = 0.25) in series that are motion-censored with replaced volumes (Methods), and residualising on it removes a fifth of the sts contrast (Results 2). The account needs only that r₁ changed; an MMI-sts contrast reports that change, whatever its origin.

old: One dataset, one drug, one parcellation, N = 14, TR 2 s, no deconvolution in the primary analysis; the DMT contrast is a proof of concept. Why r₁ fell (neural, haemodynamic, cardiac, respiratory or motion effects) is not identified; the account needs only that it did. Two redundancy functions were examined on the data, both Gaussian. On Gaussian systems every PID whose redundancy depends only on the source–target marginals reduces to MMI when the target is univariate (Barrett, 2015), which covers the lattice nodes with a single past or single future variable but not the joint-target nodes, whose target is bivariate, or the double redundancy, ΦID's own extension (Mediano et al., 2021); so "MMI-specific" is not a licensed phrase, and other Gaussian PIDs, such as CCS and the dependency-constraint PID, whose redundancy depends also on the source–source marginal (Kay & Ince, 2018), could share or not share the property. The calibration of the AR(1)-substituted estimate is on generators solved to this dataset's operating point and spectrum, not on a second dataset; the AR(1) family does not fit the data beyond lag 1 (S14 Table), the coupled family is symmetric, what acts inside the windows to produce the symmetric cross-lag departure is not identified (S9 Table), and the windowed estimator's manufacture is not removed by the substitution. The closed form, exact on the family, matches the data's atom table with each pair's measured coefficients only to within 0.053 nats for sts and 0.04 for the mirror atoms, and its exchange rate for within-pair asymmetry is a population statement that the estimators recover only in part (S10 Table). The primary contrast was planned as a test of a different hypothesis and its statistic was fixed after whole-run fits on the same data had shown a decrease; the account was derived afterwards on the same data; most later computations were entered in the record with a rule and a prediction before they were run, but not all (Methods); and several recorded predictions failed, among them the calibration's predictions for a coupling change, after which a reading of the residual was built and has been withdrawn (Methods; S19 Table). The git record establishes ordering, not blindness.

**Other Gaussian PIDs (moved from the main text's Limitations in the revision of 1–2 October 2026; Limitations now states it in a clause).** On Gaussian systems every PID whose redundancy depends only on the source–target marginals reduces to MMI when the target is univariate (Barrett, 2015), which covers the lattice nodes with a single past or single future variable but not the joint-target nodes, whose target is bivariate, or the double redundancy, ΦID's own extension (Mediano et al., 2021); so "MMI-specific" is not a licensed phrase, and other Gaussian PIDs, such as CCS and the dependency-constraint PID, whose redundancy depends also on the source–source marginal (Kay & Ince, 2018), could share or not share the property.

## 3. The closed form: checks, the coupled family, and the τ = 1 non-separability argument
why: The main text's Limitations condensed for the word limit: the sentence moved here in full.

old: ## 4. The map over (r₁, q), the overlay, the within-window regression and the regional maps
new:
**The transfer entropies on the family and at the AR(1)-substituted matrices (written for the revision of 1–2 October 2026).** A lagged measure on the same 4 × 4 matrix that contains no self-information is the pair of lag-1 Gaussian transfer entropies, I(x_t; y_{t+1} | y_t) and I(y_t; x_{t+1} | x_t). On the family both are zero: given y_t, x_t carries nothing about y_{t+1}, because the partial correlation of x_t and y_{t+1} given y_t is (a_y q − q a_y) / √((1 − q²)(1 − a_y²)) = 0, and for Gaussian variables a zero partial correlation is conditional independence. The same holds at every AR(1)-substituted matrix, whose cross-lag entries are a_y q and a_x q by construction, so on the data the lag-1 transfer entropies would be non-zero only through the departures of the measured cross-lag correlations from those values (section 6), and would be a third statistic of the lagged structure beside the directed and symmetric statistics of section 6, with the same undetermined reading; they were not computed (record, "The cold reads of 1 October 2026"). What is known of filtering concerns another quantity, Granger causality regressed on the whole past, to which transfer entropy is equivalent for Gaussian processes (Barnett & Seth, 2011, p. 406; Seth et al., 2013, p. 543). For a stationary vector autoregressive process it is invariant in population under an arbitrary invertible filter, the filtered process having in general an infinite model order, so that filtering cannot isolate causal influences within a frequency band, although in practice inferences often do change after filtering, through the increase of the empirical model order (Barnett & Seth, 2011, abstract and p. 408). Seth et al. (2013, abstract and pp. 545 and 548) show, in theory and in simulations, that Granger-causal inferences are invariant to haemodynamic convolution taken as an invertible filter, which excludes confounding onset delays, and robust to variation of the haemodynamic response, including its time to peak, but not to severe downsampling or excessive measurement noise. The lag-1 pair on the 4 × 4 matrix does not share the invariance exactly: for two AR(1) processes of the family with coefficients 0.90 and 0.70 and innovation correlation 0.3, passed through the invertible filter 1 + 0.6L + 0.3L², the two lag-1 transfer entropies are 0 before the filter and 0.0015 and 0.0004 nats after it, and 0 again to six decimals when conditioned on ten lags of the past, as the theorem requires; on the symmetric family they stay 0 (a population computation without data, made in the audit of this revision's citations, S5 Text §5: `notes/review_2026-10-01_cold_reads/audit/te_filter_check.py`). sts, which contains the two self-informations, inherits the filter's r₁ (main text, Results 1 and 7).

## 4. The map over (r₁, q), the overlay, the within-window regression and the regional maps
why: A's m10: the transfer-entropy companion stated in full, with the conditional-independence argument and the two filtering results placed where they hold: Granger causality regressed on the whole past, equivalent to transfer entropy for Gaussian processes (Barnett & Seth, 2011, abstract, p. 404, and pp. 405–406 and 408; Seth et al., 2013, abstract, p. 540, and pp. 543, 545 and 548), and not the lag-1 pair, which the audit's population check shows is not invariant (`audit/te_filter_check.py`: 0.001508 and 0.000408 nats after the filter). The main text's Results 7 names the pair and cites the two works for Granger causality under filtering.

Shading is ± 1 within-subject SEM (Cousineau, 2005; Morey, 2008): each subject's values are centred on that subject's own mean before the SEM across subjects is taken, with Morey's correction, so the bands show the uncertainty of within-subject comparisons across windows and runs and not the between-subject spread of the level, which the paper does not test; the same band is drawn on the dashed lines of (a). Grey band = pre-injection windows 1–4; hatched = window 5, excluded from the primary post set; dashed vertical line = injection at 8 min. (a) Observed whole-brain sts (solid) and the AR(1)-substituted sts (dashed): the sts of each pair's 4 × 4 matrix with its measured lag-1 autocorrelations a_x, a_y kept, its two lag-0 entries set to their mean q and its two cross-lag correlations replaced by a_y q and a_x q; DMT (red) and placebo (blue); y-range 1.00–1.30 nats. (b) The residual, observed minus AR(1)-substituted, per run, in the same units as (a) and with the same nats per unit height, so that the residual's modulation can be read against the size of the level and of the contrast. (c) The DMT − placebo difference of the residual per window (mean over subjects ± 1 within-subject SEM), with its expectation under a pure autocorrelation change as the dashed step: the pre-injection mean of the difference, then that mean plus the residual DiD that the calibration gives for an autocorrelation change of the data's size (+0.0027 ± 0.0014, condition (i) at W = 60 on the band-passed generator, S10 Table); the error bars at the post-injection window centres are the calibration's ± 1 replicate SD over its replicate datasets.
